en: Forced — …Nxh5 allows Nf7 and the black king fares no better.
The exchange drops. The Latvian stays playable in blitz, not against someone who knows this line.
We develop soundly. A gambit player must recognise the positions where the weapon simply doesn't apply.

The gambit's natural follow-up, but let's be honest: after Nb5 and Qe2, Black loses castling rights and stays under pressure. The Latvian is a surprise weapon, not a sound line — play it knowing that.
An easy system against almost everything: Bf4, e3, Bd3, c3, Nbd2. Little theory, solid plans and a kingside attack often on the menu.
London vs …d5
Jobava London — 2.Nc3
vs the fianchetto — …g6
Move orders
vs …Nf6
Jobava London — 3.Nc3
Black often starts with the knight rather than …d5. Nothing changes for us: the bishop still comes out first.
The signature move: the bishop develops BEFORE e3, never shut in.
An innocuous-looking move, played in nearly one game in four, and untreated by this repertoire.
The most played move against the London after 2.Bf4 — one player in five — and the course only saw …Nf6 and …Nc6. Black shuts in their own queen's bishop to contest the diagonal.
Black plays the London in reverse: their bishop comes out before …e6, exactly like ours. One player in seven, and the course said nothing.
The same problem in the other move order. Here the system costs even less: Bd3 is 0.05 behind c4, which is to say nothing.
The d4-e3-c3 triangle: the London structure. It is not after an opening advantage, it is after a position you can play with your eyes closed.
Black offers to trade the bishop the whole London is built on. It is their best idea against this setup.
The standard formation is complete; Bd3 follows, then Ne5 and an attack.
Keep the good bishop by sliding it to g3 rather than trading.
The knight lands on its outpost: the pivot of the London attack.
Black reroutes to f5 to challenge g3: that's the right defence — …Ne4 leaves the b7 bishop mute after the trade.
The sharper Jobava version: the knight develops first, ready for e4 or Nb5.
Black heads for the fianchetto. The engine likes e4 — but that means leaving the London for a Pirc: we stay home.
Without …a6, Black forgets the very threat this chapter announced.
Black rules out the Nb5-c7 jump before continuing.
One Black player in four plays this natural move — and it allows exactly what …a6, the only reply the course knew, was designed to prevent.
And we're back in the main line. A London player should never be thrown by the move order: the plan is identical.
Same with …e6 first: very common, and of no consequence.
Black prepares …e5 to kick the f4 bishop — the most direct plan against the London, and the course had not planned for it.
Against …g6 the London holds up well: e3, and even h4-h5 is on.
The bishop before …d5: four Black players in five do this, and the chapter started from the other order.
The queen prepares long castling: this is the sharp Jobava, with a kingside attack to follow.
The h4-h5 rush aims straight at the enemy castled king — the London has teeth.
The pesky move: the queen hits b2. You must know the reply.
Develop while threatening Nb5; grabbing b2 becomes very risky for Black.
Too greedy: grabbing b2 lets the queen get trapped.
The refutation: Nb5 threatens the Nc7+ fork, and the b2-queen is short of squares. Avoid it as Black!
The natural defence — and a losing one. See the other line for …Nd5, the only move that holds.
THE move to know from both sides: the knight covers c7 and reopens a square for the queen. The trap does not win by force.
The real move: a3 shuts the a2 square BEFORE Rb1. In the other order, 6.Rb1 Qxa2 and the queen slips away.
Repetition: White keeps a small initiative, nothing more. The real win only comes against 5…Na6.
Main line once again. Nf3, c3, Nbd2 follow.
The very same position as the main anti-fianchetto chapter. Nothing new: e3 then h4-h5.
One game in two goes through this castling, and the chapter jumped straight to …d5. Black's king is home; ours will follow.
One game in three: Black delays …d5 and keeps the options open. The course only knew …d5 and castling.
The bishop comes out, as always. The position stays balanced — and it plays with familiar landmarks.
Opposite castling, sharp play. We know where to strike; the opponent often doesn't yet.
The immediate pin, one game in four — and the course only had …d5.
Here is the whole point of the Jobava London: the knight jumps at c7, where king and rook cross. Black must react at once, and every reply concedes something.
Consolidate without hurrying: the a6 knight is offside and the lead in development is lasting.
The bishop comes out before we have played Bd3: the most awkward move in the whole course, played one time in three here.
THE move to know: Black wants to trade off our good bishop. Don't lose track of it on h5.
The bishop steps back and keeps the diagonal. We never trade it willingly — it's the piece the system is named for.
Recapture towards the centre AND open the h-file. The trade Black wanted has done us a favour.
Three games in ten: Black develops without hurrying …c5. The course only planned for the push.
An in-between check before deciding: we gain a tempo and force Black to commit before we take on d6.
Since Black developed the bishop instead of holding the centre, we hit d5 at once: this is the moment when that move is worth the most.
The “Jobava” version: we develop towards the centre instead of retreating for safety. If Black plays …e5 we answer d5, and the bishop finds another diagonal.
We close instead of trading: Black is left with a d7 knight without a square and an f8 bishop waiting behind its own pawns.
A knight retreat that surprises, and yet makes sense: the c3 knight has nothing left to do there, so it heads back to d2 and then f3 or b3, depending on which wing the game turns on.
Black finally kicks the knight, but a tempo too late: the position has opened in our favour while they were busy with it.
The small but necessary move: without it, …Bg4 pins the knight and our f4 bishop loses its support.
Be2 rather than Bc4: the engine prefers Bc4 by a tenth of a pawn, then brings it back to e2 two moves later. A bishop that goes out and comes back teaches nothing.
We offer the trade anyway. The engine prefers c4 (+0.44 against +0.30) — but c4 leaves the system this course teaches, and 0.14 of a pawn is not worth a repertoire that contradicts itself.
Black nearly always takes: keeping the bishop would cost a tempo and leave Bxf5 available at the right moment.
NOW c4, and not on move four: the light-squared bishops are gone, so the push no longer leaves us holes on b5 or e4.
Recapture with the c-pawn, not the queen: the c-file opens for the rook and d3 reinforces e4. That is the difference from the …Nc6 line.

The queen defends c3 and prepares castling long. To be blunt: it is the best move, and it yields only equality (−0.06). Against this pin the Jobava promises nothing — better to know that before the game than after.
Black hits the centre while our king is still in the middle.
The system, no hesitation: e3, then Bd3 and c4 in due course. Here the engine agrees.
We decline the trade: our bishop is worth more than his, and on g3 it still watches e5.
Deliberate imbalance: White's centre versus Black's queenside majority and a biting g7 bishop. Tactical, risky, but full of counterplay with …b5.
Classical Main Line
Taimanov — 7.f4 Bb5+
Fianchetto Variation — g3
Modern Line — 7.h3
The Modern Benoni assumes 2.c4 c5 3.d5: without c4, White won't push d5 and the pawn-chain structure never appears.
White closes; the Benoni structure takes shape.
Striking d5 to open the e-file and fix the signature structure.
The feared Taimanov Attack: White threatens e4-e5 to sweep the centre.
The modern line: h3 takes away …Bg4 and prepares Bd3, Nf3 while keeping everything solid.
The precise check before setting up the centre. …Nfd7 is the main reply.
The fianchetto: calmer, positional play; the g2 bishop watches d5 and b7.
Without c4, …c5 leads nowhere: we build a classical structure and wait. If c4 comes later, the Benoni is back on.
Even more flexible than the Pirc: fianchetto without …Nf6 to keep every option. Give up the centre, then hit with …c5, …b5 or …e5.
Tiger's Modern — …a6 …b5
Austrian — 4.f4
Gurgenidze System — …c6 …d5
3.Nf3 — slow development
Over a quarter of games, and the course started from 2.d4. White keeps the centre flexible to dodge our counterattack.
Nearly four games in ten here, and the chapter went elsewhere. Without Nc3, White gives up on the direct attack.
The big centre; Black harasses it with …Nf6, …Na6-c7 and …c5.
White aims for Bh6 and 0-0-0; Black counters fast on the queenside with …b5.
Against f4, the Gurgenidze hits …d5: close the centre and target e5/f4.
We strike before they establish d4: it becomes a Sicilian with the fianchetto already decided — favourable ground for us.
The break at the right moment: the f4 bishop no longer guards d4 and the c-file opens for us.
One of the most reliable defences in chess: …Bb4 pins the c3 knight to inflict doubled pawns and control e4. If White avoids Nc3, the Queen's Indian takes over.
Nimzo — Rubinstein 4.e3
Nimzo — Classical 4.Qc2
Nimzo — Sämisch 4.a3
Nimzo — 4.f3
Queen's Indian — 3.Nf3 b6
One game in six. No c4, so no Nimzo: the …Bb4 pin would have nothing to pin.
White sidesteps the …Bb4 pin. Black switches to the Queen's Indian.
The Nimzowitsch pin: the threat of …Bxc3 weighs on White's structure and on e4.
Rubinstein, the most solid and most played line.
The Classical: White wants to recapture on c3 with the queen and avoid doubled pawns.
The Sämisch: White grabs the bishop pair at once, at the cost of doubled pawns.
White wants e4 at all costs. The energetic reply is …d5 in the centre.
The queen's bishop fianchettoes to b7 and contests e4 from afar.
The move that makes the London uncomfortable: the queen hits b2, which the bishop — gone to f4 — no longer defends. Same spirit as the Nimzo: annoy before developing.
We keep every option: if c4 comes, the Nimzo is back on via …e6; otherwise we have a sound Queen's Gambit structure.
Taking is correct here: with no knight on c3, White needs an extra tempo to regain the pawn.
1.b3: the queen's bishop fianchettoes to b2 and eyes the centre and Black's king along the long diagonal. Little theory, very logical, often tricky.
vs …e5
vs …Nf6/…g6
The bishop heads for b2: the whole strategy revolves around the a1-h8 diagonal.
Black props up e5 with the pawn rather than the knight, keeping c6 free. One game in five, and the chapter started from …Nc6.
The most played move here — one game in two — and the chapter started from …Nf6. Black builds a big centre: precisely what the b2 bishop is waiting for.
Black puts the bishop on its most aggressive diagonal before …Nf6. The course planned for …Nf6 and …d5, not this.
Pressing c6 to undermine the defender of e5, the b2 bishop's target.
The most played move in the whole chapter — 47 % of games here — and it had no answer at all.
Black prepares …e5, to occupy the diagonal rather than suffer it. The chapter only saw …Nf6.
The double centre pawn: Black grabs space and denies us the diagonal. The chapter only knew …Nf6 and …Nc6.
Solid and unfussy: Black shuts the diagonal with a pawn. We transpose into the same structure as …Nf6, one move earlier.
The good bishop comes out before …e6 — the golden rule of these structures, and Black follows it.
Since Black has passed on an immediate …c5, we take the centre for good.
The most played reply in the whole repertoire — almost one game in four — and the chapter only saw …g6. Black keeps everything open: …b6, …c5 or …d5, depending on what we do.
Black occupies the centre instead of contesting it from afar. One player in six, and the chapter had not planned for it.
Black chooses the King's Indian structure rather than …d5. The course only knew immediate castling.
Two Black players in three castle here, and the chapter continued with Be2. Taking the centre is more ambitious: the g7 bishop runs into a wall.
The same idea as ever: undermine c6, the defender of e5. Black's centre only looks impressive while it holds.
Black kicks the bishop — and does us a favour: after the trade, their c-pawns are doubled.
We stop …e5 with a developing move: the knight covers the square and concedes nothing.
The most natural developing move, one game in three — and the course only answered …f6, which is rare.
The other frequent move here: the pin before development.
…f6 has blocked the g8 knight's exit and loosened the light squares. We have the centre and the better game.
Fianchettos facing off on the long diagonal: the game will turn on who controls d5 and e5.
We stay non-committal too. The knight comes out, e5 stays covered, and the choice of structure waits one more move.
Two fianchettos facing each other. The difference is that we took the centre: the b7 bishop runs into d4-e3, ours breathes.
The repertoire's motif: press c6 to undermine the defender of Black's centre.
The surprising move: after …d6 the bishop no longer hits e5, so we occupy the centre instead. The position becomes a Closed Sicilian where WE are the ones with a bishop on b2.
Black goes for counterplay — and opens the b2 bishop's diagonal at the same time as their own.
Doubled pawns on an open file, king still in the centre: the b2 bishop finally has a target.
No hurry with d4: first open the king's bishop, and keep d4 as a break for later.
Only now. Black must choose: keep the tension, or take — and the exchange leaves them facing an isolated pawn.
The move to remember: we chase the f5 bishop, the piece holding the light squares. The knight returns to f3 as soon as its job is done.
The system, unchanged: b3, Bb2, e3, Nf3. The long diagonal is already there; it remains to finish developing.
Here we take the centre: the g4 bishop has stopped watching d4, so we occupy the square while it is free.
Black gives up the bishop pair to loosen our grip on e5 — the standard trade-off in this line.
Opposite castling on both sides: the game turns into a race, and our b2 bishop is already pointing the right way.
The indirect pin: we attack the defender of e5 rather than the pawn itself. The Larsen's standard reply to …Nc6.
Black has to take: allowing dxe5 would open the long diagonal onto their king.

On e2, NOT f3. This is the point to remember from the whole line: with Black's pawn on e5 and knight on f6, Nf3 invites …e4, which gains a tempo and space. Measured: Ne2 +0.25, Nf3 −0.10. The course played Nf3 everywhere out of habit; here the habit costs a third of a pawn.
We trade at a moment of our choosing: the doubled c6/c7 pawns hamper …d5, and our b2 bishop eyes the weakened square.
Against a fianchetto we take the big centre: the b2 and g7 bishops stare at each other, and whoever has more pawns in the centre wins that duel.
We gain queenside space before …e5 arrives: the natural plan once the centre locks up.
A hypermodern surprise weapon: 1…Nc6 invites White to push d4-d5, then Black harasses that centre. Its big plus: opponents rarely know the theory.
2.d4 d5 3.e5 (advance)
2.Nf3 — the most common move
2.d4 d5 — the main line
The Nimzowitsch move: the knight comes out before the pawns, ready to bite the centre.
The course's main hole: four games in ten, and no answer at all. The student left the repertoire at move two.
Strike e4 at once; the game turns concrete.
The advance closes the centre; Black's bishop comes to f5 before …e6, as in an Advance Caro-Kann.
